title: The Dynamic Method
body_html:
The Dynamic Method

The dynamic method (also called the cocharacter construction of parabolic subgroups) is a scheme-theoretic technique for producing parabolic subgroups and their Levi decompositions from a single cocharacter \(\lambda : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\). It is the modern replacement for ad hoc inductive constructions.

Setup

Let \(G\) be a connected reductive group over a field \(F\), and let \(\lambda : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) be a cocharacter (a group homomorphism from the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{G}_m\) to \(G\)). Conjugation by \(\lambda(t)\) gives an action of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) on \(G\) by automorphisms, inducing a weight decomposition.

Definition of the three subgroups

For a cocharacter \(\lambda : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\), define three subgroup schemes of \(G\):

Parabolic \(P(\lambda)\): the functor on \(F\)-algebras \[ P(\lambda)(R) \;:=\; \bigl\{g \in G(R) : \lim_{t \to 0} \lambda(t)\, g\, \lambda(t)^{-1} \text{ exists in } G(R)\bigr\}, \] where the limit means the morphism \(\mathbb{G}_m \to G\) defined by \(t \mapsto \lambda(t) g \lambda(t)^{-1}\) extends to a morphism \(\mathbb{A}^1 \to G\).

Unipotent radical \(U(\lambda)\): \[ U(\lambda)(R) \;:=\; \bigl\{g \in G(R) : \lim_{t \to 0} \lambda(t)\, g\, \lambda(t)^{-1} = 1\bigr\}. \]

Levi subgroup \(L(\lambda)\): \[ L(\lambda) \;:=\; Z_G(\lambda) \;=\; \bigl\{g \in G : \lambda(t)\, g\, \lambda(t)^{-1} = g \text{ for all } t\bigr\}, \] the centralizer of the image of \(\lambda\).

Main theorem

Theorem (SGA3 Exposé XXVI §1; Kaletha-Prasad Proposition 2.11.20). Let \(G\) be a connected reductive group over \(F\) and \(\lambda : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) a cocharacter.

  1. \(P(\lambda)\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).
  2. \(U(\lambda)\) is the unipotent radical \(R_u(P(\lambda))\).
  3. \(L(\lambda)\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P(\lambda)\), and there is a semidirect product decomposition \[ P(\lambda) \;=\; L(\lambda) \;\ltimes\; U(\lambda). \]
  4. The opposite parabolic \(P(\lambda)^- := P(-\lambda)\) satisfies \(P(\lambda) \cap P(-\lambda) = L(\lambda)\).
  5. Every parabolic subgroup of \(G\) arises as \(P(\lambda)\) for some cocharacter \(\lambda\).

Weight decomposition on the Lie algebra

The cocharacter \(\lambda\) gives a weight space decomposition of the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G)\): \[ \mathfrak{g} \;=\; \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathfrak{g}_n, \quad \mathfrak{g}_n := \{X \in \mathfrak{g} : \operatorname{Ad}(\lambda(t)) X = t^n X\}. \]

Then: \[ \operatorname{Lie}(P(\lambda)) = \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \mathfrak{g}_n, \quad \operatorname{Lie}(U(\lambda)) = \bigoplus_{n > 0} \mathfrak{g}_n, \quad \operatorname{Lie}(L(\lambda)) = \mathfrak{g}_0. \]

Relation to root subgroups

If \(T\) is a maximal torus containing the image of \(\lambda\) (always possible after conjugation), the weight spaces \(\mathfrak{g}_n\) decompose further by root spaces. The roots \(\alpha \in \Phi(G, T)\) with \(\langle \alpha, \lambda \rangle > 0\) contribute to \(\operatorname{Lie}(U(\lambda))\), those with \(\langle \alpha, \lambda \rangle = 0\) to \(\operatorname{Lie}(L(\lambda))\), and those with \(\langle \alpha, \lambda \rangle < 0\) to \(\operatorname{Lie}(U(-\lambda))\).

For the standard cocharacter \(\lambda = \varpi^\vee\) (a coroot evaluated at a uniformiser), this gives the affine root filtration used in Bruhat-Tits theory.

Examples

Standard parabolics of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\)

Take \(G = \mathrm{GL}_n\) with diagonal maximal torus \(T\). For the cocharacter \(\lambda : t \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(t^{k_1}, \ldots, t^{k_n})\) with \(k_1 \ge k_2 \ge \cdots \ge k_n\), the resulting \(P(\lambda)\) is the standard upper-triangular block parabolic for the partition given by the consecutive equal blocks of \(k_i\).

The Iwasawa decomposition

For a reductive group over a local field, the dynamic method for the cocharacter \(\lambda = \varpi^\vee\) (uniformiser cocharacter) recovers the Iwahori-Hecke filtration of parahoric subgroups; cf.\ valued root data.

Applications

  • Classification of parabolics. Every parabolic is of the form \(P(\lambda)\), giving a bijection between \(G(k)\)-conjugacy classes of parabolics and \(W\)-orbits of cocharacters (for \(G\) split).
  • Integral models. Over the integers, the dynamic method gives smooth affine group scheme models for parabolics: \(P(\lambda)\) extends to a smooth \(\mathcal{O}_F\)-group scheme (parahoric group schemes).
  • Unipotent radicals. The unipotent radical \(U(\lambda)\) is split unipotent and admits a filtration by weight spaces — used in the Moy-Prasad theory.
